claim: Ubp15 is a deubiquitylase that regulates nuclear export in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Here we identified deubiquitylase Ubp15 as a regulator of nuclear export in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Ubp15 interacts with RNA polymerase II.
source: Ubp15 interacts with both RNA polymerase II and the nuclear pore complex, and its deletion reverts the nuclear export defect of E3 ligase Rsp5 mutants.
evidence: This interaction is demonstrated through proteomic analysis and confirmed by reciprocal affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ubp15 interacts with the nuclear pore complex.
source: Ubp15 interacts with both RNA polymerase II and the nuclear pore complex, and its deletion reverts the nuclear export defect of E3 ligase Rsp5 mutants.
evidence: Reciprocal affinity purification of Ubp15 revealed enrichment of almost the entire NPC as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of UBP15 reverts the nuclear export defect of E3 ligase Rsp5 mutants.
source: Ubp15 interacts with both RNA polymerase II and the nuclear pore complex, and its deletion reverts the nuclear export defect of E3 ligase Rsp5 mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA FISH experiments showing that deletion of UBP15 suppressed the mRNA export defect of the rsp5-1 mutant (Figure 4D).

claim: Deletion of UBP15 leads to hyper-ubiquitylation of the main nuclear export receptor Mex67.
source: The deletion of UBP15 leads to hyper-ubiquitylation of the main nuclear export receptor Mex67 and affects its association with THO, a complex coupling transcription to mRNA processing and involved in the recruitment of mRNA export factors to nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is shown through in vivo ubiquitylation assays presented in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Deletion of UBP15 affects Mex67 association with THO complex.
source: The deletion of UBP15 leads to hyper-ubiquitylation of the main nuclear export receptor Mex67 and affects its association with THO, a complex coupling transcription to mRNA processing and involved in the recruitment of mRNA export factors to nascent transcripts.
evidence: Proteomic analysis of Mex67 complexes showed that all four subunits of THO were less associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells (Figure 5D).

claim: THO is a complex coupling transcription to mRNA processing and involved in the recruitment of mRNA export factors to nascent transcripts.
source: The deletion of UBP15 leads to hyper-ubiquitylation of the main nuclear export receptor Mex67 and affects its association with THO, a complex coupling transcription to mRNA processing and involved in the recruitment of mRNA export factors to nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about THO function cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rpb1, the largest subunit of RNAPII, contains a C-terminal domain (CTD) composed of 26 to 52 repetitions of the heptapeptide Y1S2P3T4S5P6S7 in yeast and mammals, respectively.
source: Rpb1, the largest subunit of RNAPII, contains a C-terminal domain (CTD) composed of 26 to 52 repetitions (in yeast and mammals, respectively) of the heptapeptide Y1S2P3T4S5P6S7 (Chapman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Chapman et al., 2008.

claim: The CTD of RNAPII is highly conserved and essential for viability in all organisms.
source: The CTD is highly conserved and essential for the viability in all organisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CTD.

claim: During transcription, the CTD is extensively and dynamically phosphorylated to coordinate the binding of proteins involved in the different steps of transcription and to couple transcription to mRNA processing.
source: During transcription, the CTD is extensively and dynamically phosphorylated to coordinate the binding of proteins involved in the different steps of transcription and to couple transcription to mRNA processing (Corden, 2013; Eick and Geyer, 2013; Harlen and Churchman, 2017; Jeronimo et al., 2013; Jeronimo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pre-mRNAs and mature mRNAs are packaged with RNA-binding proteins to form dynamic ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) during their synthesis, processing and export.
source: During their synthesis, processing and export, pre-mRNAs and mature mRNAs are packaged with RNA-binding proteins to form dynamic ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) (Mitchell and Parker, 2014; Singh et al., 2015; Tutucci and Stutz, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchell and Parker, 2014; Singh et al., 2015; Tutucci and Stutz, 2011.

claim: The mRNA export machinery is highly conserved from yeast to humans and mainly depends on the export factor Mex67-Mtr2 (TAP-NXF1 in mammals).
source: The mRNA export machinery is highly conserved from yeast to humans and mainly depends on the export factor Mex67-Mtr2 (TAP-NXF1 in mammals) (Niño et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2019; Wende et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Niño et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2019; Wende et al., 2019.

claim: Mex67, in complex with Mtr2, mediates transport through the nuclear pore complex (NPC) via interactions with several FG-enriched nucleoporins (Nups).
source: Mex67, in complex with Mtr2, mediates transport through the nuclear pore complex (NPC) via interactions with several FG-enriched nucleoporins (Nups) (Santos-Rosa et al., 1998; Strässer et al., 2000a; Terry et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Santos-Rosa et al., 1998; Strässer et al., 2000a; Terry et al., 2007.

claim: Yra1 (ALY/REF in mammals) is the first adaptor to intervene by facilitating the recruitment of Mex67 to the mRNP.
source: Yra1 (ALY/REF in mammals) is the first adaptor to intervein by facilitating the recruitment of Mex67 to the mRNP (Strässer and Hurt, 2000b; Zenklusen et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Strässer and Hurt, 2000b; Zenklusen et al., 2001.

claim: Nab2 has been reported to form a complex with Mex67 and Yra1.
source: while Nab2 has been reported to form a complex with Mex67 and Yra1 (Batisse et al., 2009; Iglesias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Batisse et al., 2009; Iglesias et al., 2010.

claim: An excess of Nab2 can bypass the loss of Yra1.
source: Interestingly, an excess of Nab2 can bypass the loss of Yra1 (Iglesias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iglesias et al., 2010.

claim: Npl3, an RNA-binding protein, directly interacts with Mex67 and participates in mRNA nuclear export.
source: Npl3, an RNA-binding protein, also directly interacts with Mex67 and participates in mRNA nuclear export (Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 1996.

claim: TREX is a protein complex composed of THO (Hpr1, Tho2, Mft1, and Thp2), the Mex67 adapters Yra1 and the DEAD-box ATPase Sub2.
source: Indeed, TREX, a protein complex composed of THO (Hpr1, Tho2, Mft1, and Thp2), the Mex67 adapters Yra1 and the DEAD-box ATPase Sub2 (Strässer et al., 2002), is recruited to the transcribing RNAPII and helps in the assembly of an export competent mRNP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Strässer et al., 2002.

claim: TREX is recruited to the transcribing RNAPII and helps in the assembly of an export competent mRNP.
source: Indeed, TREX, a protein complex composed of THO (Hpr1, Tho2, Mft1, and Thp2), the Mex67 adapters Yra1 and the DEAD-box ATPase Sub2 (Strässer et al., 2002), is recruited to the transcribing RNAPII and helps in the assembly of an export competent mRNP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Strässer et al., 2002.

claim: THO recruitment to active chromatin is facilitated by the Tho2 subunit.
source: THO recruitment to active chromatin is facilitated by the Tho2 subunit (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peña et al., 2012.

claim: Hpr1 binds Sub2 on nascent transcripts and is implicated in the early recruitment of Mex67, an interaction mediated by a ubiquitin-dependent process.
source: Then, Hpr1 binds Sub2 on nascent transcripts and is implicated in the early recruitment of Mex67, an interaction mediated by a ubiquitin-dependent process (Gwizdek et al., 2005; Gwizdek et al., 2006; Zenklusen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gwizdek et al., 2005; Gwizdek et al., 2006; Zenklusen et al., 2002.

claim: Yra1 is co-transcriptionally recruited, notably by the cap binding complex (CBC).
source: Yra1 is also co-transcriptionally recruited, notably by the cap binding complex (CBC) (Cheng et al., 2006; Sen et al., 2019; Viphakone et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2006; Sen et al., 2019; Viphakone et al., 2019.

claim: Yra1 is transferred to Sub2.
source: and transferred to Sub2 (Johnson et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2011.

claim: TREX-2 (Sac3, Thp1, Sus1, Cdc31, and Sem1) interacts with the nuclear side of the NPC and participates in the coordination between transcription and mRNA export.
source: Later, TREX-2 (Sac3, Thp1, Sus1, Cdc31, and Sem1) interacts with the nuclear side of the NPC and participates in the coordination between transcription and mRNA export (Cabal et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2004; Jani et al., 2009; Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cabal et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2004; Jani et al., 2009; Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2004.

claim: Yra1 is removed from mRNP complexes before exiting the nucleus.
source: In contrast to Yra1, which is removed from mRNP complexes before exiting the nucleus (Lund and Guthrie, 2005), Nab2 and Npl3 translocate together with the mRNP and are released at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC (Tran et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lund and Guthrie, 2005.

claim: Nab2 and Npl3 translocate together with the mRNP and are released at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC.
source: In contrast to Yra1, which is removed from mRNP complexes before exiting the nucleus (Lund and Guthrie, 2005), Nab2 and Npl3 translocate together with the mRNP and are released at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC (Tran et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tran et al., 2007.

claim: Once the mRNA reaches the cytoplasm, Nup159 and Nup42 NPC subunits recruit two essential mRNA export factors, the DEAD-box ATPase Dbp5 and its ATPase activator Gle1, which are in charge of remodeling and disassembling the mRNPs emerging from the NPC.
source: Once the mRNA reaches the cytoplasm, Nup159 and Nup42 NPC subunits recruit two essential mRNA export factors, the DEAD-box ATPase Dbp5 and its ATPase activator Gle1, which are in charge of remodeling and disassembling the mRNPs emerging from the NPC (Adams et al., 2017; Hodge et al., 2011; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Weirich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adams et al., 2017; Hodge et al., 2011; Lund and Guthrie, 2005; Weirich et al., 2006.

claim: Disassembly of the mRNP in the cytoplasm prevents its return to the nucleus, resulting in unidirectional mRNA translocation.
source: Disassembly of the mRNP in the cytoplasm prevents its return to the nucleus, resulting in unidirectional mRNA translocation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the described mechanism.

claim: The release of mRNA export factors allows them to return to the nucleus where they can function in additional rounds of mRNA export.
source: In addition, the release of mRNA export factors allow them to return to the nucleus where they can function in additional rounds of mRNA export (Stewart, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stewart, 2007.

claim: Dbp5 does not affect the interaction of Mex67 with the NPC.
source: Recently, it was shown that Dbp5 does not affect the interaction of Mex67 with the NPC.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Derrer et al., 2019.

claim: Mex67 does not translocate to the cytoplasmic face of the NPC with the mRNPs but rather functions as a mobile nucleoporin, facilitating their translocation to the cytoplasm.
source: Instead, it was proposed that Mex67 does not translocate to the cytoplasmic face of the NPC with the mRNPs but rather functions as a mobile nucleoporin, facilitating their translocation to the cytoplasm (Derrer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Derrer et al., 2019.

claim: The Rsp5 ubiquitin ligase was shown to target RNAPII for degradation during DNA damage.
source: The Rsp5 ubiquitin ligase was shown to target RNAPII for degradation during DNA damage (Beaudenon et al., 1999; Huibregtse et al., 1997; Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaudenon et al., 1999; Huibregtse et al., 1997; Wu et al., 2001.

claim: Ubiquitylation of RNAPII in human cells was shown to play a role in transcription-coupled repair.
source: More recently, ubiquitylation of RNAPII in human cells was shown to play a role in transcription-coupled repair (Nakazawa et al., 2020; Tufegdžić Vidaković et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakazawa et al., 2020; Tufegdžić Vidaković et al., 2020.

claim: RNAPII was shown to be ubiquitylated in vivo by the ubiquitin ligase Asr1.
source: RNAPII was also shown to be ubiquitylated in vivo by the ubiquitin ligase Asr1 (Daulny et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daulny et al., 2008.

claim: Ubiquitylation of RNAPII by Asr1 occurs on transcribed genes and leads to the dissociation of two RNAPII subunits (Rpb4/7), a process involved in the silencing of subtelomeric genes.
source: In this case, the ubiquitylation occurs on transcribed genes and leads to the dissociation of two RNAPII subunits (Rpb4/7), a process involved in the silencing of subtelomeric genes (McCann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCann et al., 2016.

claim: Ubiquitylation is involved in mRNA export.
source: Ubiquitylation is also involved in mRNA export (Babour et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Babour et al., 2012.

claim: The THO component Hpr1 is poly-ubiquitylated by Rsp5, which facilitates the co-transcriptional recruitment of the mRNA export factor Mex67, via its ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain.
source: The THO component Hpr1 is poly-ubiquitylated by Rsp5, which facilitates the co-transcriptional recruitment of the mRNA export factor Mex67, via its ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain (Gwizdek et al., 2005; Gwizdek et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gwizdek et al., 2005; Gwizdek et al., 2006.

claim: The ubiquitin E3 ligase Tom1 is required for ubiquitylation of the Mex67 adaptor Yra1, which promotes its dissociation from mRNP complexes before export to the cytoplasm.
source: The ubiquitin E3 ligase Tom1 is required for ubiquitylation of the Mex67 adaptor Yra1, which promotes its dissociation from mRNP complexes before export to the cytoplasm (Iglesias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iglesias et al., 2010.

claim: H2B ubiquitylation facilitates the assembly of Mex67, Yra1, Nab2, and Npl3 into mRNPs.
source: H2B ubiquitylation, a histone modification deposited on genes co-transcriptionally, facilitates the assembly of Mex67, Yra1, Nab2, and Npl3 into mRNPs (Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012.

claim: H2B ubiquitylation mediates the assembly of Npl3 directly.
source: Interestingly, while H2B ubiquitylation mediates the assembly of Npl3 directly, its effect on Mex67, Yra1, Nab2 assembly onto mRNPs involves the ubiquitylation of Swd2, a subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation factor (CPF), connecting chromatin to transcriptional termination and mRNA export (Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012.

claim: H2B ubiquitylation's effect on Mex67, Yra1, Nab2 assembly onto mRNPs involves the ubiquitylation of Swd2, a subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation factor (CPF), connecting chromatin to transcriptional termination and mRNA export.
source: Interestingly, while H2B ubiquitylation mediates the assembly of Npl3 directly, its effect on Mex67, Yra1, Nab2 assembly onto mRNPs involves the ubiquitylation of Swd2, a subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation factor (CPF), connecting chromatin to transcriptional termination and mRNA export (Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vitaliano-Prunier et al., 2012.

claim: More than 50% of Nups can be ubiquitylated.
source: Moreover, a systematic analysis of NPC ubiquitylation was conducted in yeast and showed that more than 50% of Nups can be ubiquitylated (Hayakawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hayakawa et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquitylation of Nups does not influence Nups localization within the NPC.
source: As this modification does not influence Nups localization within the NPC, it is tempting to speculate that it might regulate the interaction with the Mex67 UBA domain during mRNA export.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hayakawa et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquitylation of Nups might regulate the interaction with the Mex67 UBA domain during mRNA export.
source: As this modification does not influence Nups localization within the NPC, it is tempting to speculate that it might regulate the interaction with the Mex67 UBA domain during mRNA export.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The association of Ubp15 with RNAPII increased in a mutant for the CTD phosphatase Fcp1.
source: The association of Ubp15 with RNAPII increased in a mutant for the CTD phosphatase Fcp1, suggesting a role in transcriptional elongation.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 rescued the sensitivity of transcription elongation factor mutants to 6-azauracil (6AU).
source: Furthermore, the deletion of UBP15 rescued the sensitivity of transcription elongation factor mutants to 6-azauracil (6AU), an inhibitor of transcription elongation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the serial-dilution growth assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 did not rescue the transcription elongation processivity defect of dst1Δ cells in the presence of 6AU.
source: While these experiments functionally connect Ubp15 to transcription elongation, the deletion of UBP15 did not rescue the transcription elongation processivity defect of dst1Δ cells in the presence of 6AU, suggesting that the link between Ubp15 and elongation may be indirect.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-qPCR and ChIP-chip experiments presented in Figure 3.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 rescued the thermosensitivity of a mutant for RSP5.
source: The deletion of UBP15 rescued the thermosensitivity of a mutant for RSP5, an E3 ligase involved in DNA damage and mRNA export.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the serial-dilution growth assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 suppressed the mRNA export defect of rsp5 mutants.
source: Interestingly, the deletion of UBP15 suppressed the mRNA export defect of rsp5 mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ubp15 regulates the ubiquitylation of Mex67.
source: Finally, we showed that Ubp15 regulates the ubiquitylation of Mex67, which in turn regulates its interaction with THO, a complex involved in mRNA processing and export.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo ubiquitylation assays shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Mex67 ubiquitylation regulates its interaction with THO.
source: Finally, we showed that Ubp15 regulates the ubiquitylation of Mex67, which in turn regulates its interaction with THO, a complex involved in mRNA processing and export.
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic analysis of Mex67 complexes shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Fcp1 is a major CTD phosphatase and its mutation leads to increased CTD phosphorylation at serines 2, 5, and 7.
source: Fcp1 is a major CTD phosphatase and its mutation leads to increased CTD phosphorylation at serines 2, 5, and 7 (Bataille et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bataille et al., 2012.

claim: Ubp15 is a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis.
source: One RNAPII-interacting protein identified in this experiment is Ubp15, a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis (Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010), progression into the S phase (Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015), peroxisomal export (Debelyy et al., 2011), and methylmercury susceptibility (Hwang et al., 2012), but with no known roles in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010.

claim: Ubp15 is known for its role in progression into the S phase.
source: One RNAPII-interacting protein identified in this experiment is Ubp15, a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis (Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010), progression into the S phase (Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015), peroxisomal export (Debelyy et al., 2011), and methylmercury susceptibility (Hwang et al., 2012), but with no known roles in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015.

claim: Ubp15 is known for its role in peroxisomal export.
source: One RNAPII-interacting protein identified in this experiment is Ubp15, a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis (Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010), progression into the S phase (Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015), peroxisomal export (Debelyy et al., 2011), and methylmercury susceptibility (Hwang et al., 2012), but with no known roles in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Debelyy et al., 2011.

claim: Ubp15 is known for its role in methylmercury susceptibility.
source: One RNAPII-interacting protein identified in this experiment is Ubp15, a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis (Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010), progression into the S phase (Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015), peroxisomal export (Debelyy et al., 2011), and methylmercury susceptibility (Hwang et al., 2012), but with no known roles in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hwang et al., 2012.

claim: Ubp15 had no known roles in transcription prior to this study.
source: One RNAPII-interacting protein identified in this experiment is Ubp15, a deubiquitylase known for its role in the regulation of endocytosis (Ho et al., 2017; Kouranti et al., 2010), progression into the S phase (Álvarez et al., 2016; Ostapenko et al., 2015), peroxisomal export (Debelyy et al., 2011), and methylmercury susceptibility (Hwang et al., 2012), but with no known roles in transcription.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the text.

claim: The association of Ubp15 with RNAPII is increased in the fcp1-1 mutant, suggesting it is recruited (directly or indirectly) to the elongating polymerase via CTD phosphorylation.
source: The association of Ubp15 with RNAPII is increased in the fcp1-1 mutant, suggesting it is recruited (directly or indirectly) to the elongating polymerase via CTD phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ubp15 interacts with the phosphorylated form of RNAPII.
source: This experiment confirmed the interaction between Ubp15 and the phosphorylated form of RNAPII (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is confirmed by western blot shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The histone chaperone and elongation factor FACT (Spt16 and Pob3) is enriched in RNAPII purified from fcp1-1 cells.
source: Interestingly, the histone chaperone and elongation factor FACT (Spt16 and Pob3) is also enriched in RNAPII purified from fcp1-1 cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis and western blot presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both FACT and Rpb1 are substrates of Ubp15 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: and both FACT and Rpb1 are substrates of Ubp15 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Beckley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beckley et al., 2015.

claim: The association of Asr1, a ubiquitin ligase known to bind the CTD and to ubiquitylate RNAPII in the context of elongation, is decreased in fcp1-1 cells.
source: In addition, the association of Asr1, a ubiquitin ligase known to bind the CTD and to ubiquitylate RNAPII in the context of elongation (Daulny et al., 2008; McCann et al., 2016), is decreased in fcp1-1 cells (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis presented in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 6-azauracil (6AU) is an inhibitor of GTP biosynthesis commonly used to test for mutations that affect transcriptional elongation.
source: First, we looked for sensitivity to 6-azauracil (6AU), an inhibitor of GTP biosynthesis commonly used to test for mutations that affect transcriptional elongation (Riles et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riles et al., 2004.

claim: The ubp15Δ mutant did not show significant sensitivity to 6AU on its own.
source: While the ubp15Δ mutant did not show significant sensitivity to 6AU on its own, it rescued the 6AU sensitivity of several elongation factor mutants including dst1Δ (TFIIS), spt4Δ and spt5-CTRΔ (DSIF), spt6-1004 and hpr1Δ (THO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The ubp15Δ mutation rescued the 6AU sensitivity of dst1Δ (TFIIS), spt4Δ and spt5-CTRΔ (DSIF), spt6-1004 and hpr1Δ (THO) mutants.
source: While the ubp15Δ mutant did not show significant sensitivity to 6AU on its own, it rescued the 6AU sensitivity of several elongation factor mutants including dst1Δ (TFIIS), spt4Δ and spt5-CTRΔ (DSIF), spt6-1004 and hpr1Δ (THO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The 6AU sensitivity of bur2Δ, ctk1Δ, rtf1Δ, and cdc73Δ mutants was not affected by the deletion of UBP15.
source: Interestingly, the 6AU sensitivity of other elongation factors such as bur2Δ, ctk1Δ, rtf1Δ, and cdc73Δ mutants was not affected by the deletion of UBP15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ubp15-C214A mutant, but not the WT UBP15, rescued the dst1Δ and spt4Δ sensitivities to 6AU.
source: The ubp15-C214A mutant, but not the WT UBP15, rescued the dst1Δ and spt4Δ sensitivities to 6AU (Figure 2B), demonstrating that the effect of Ubp15 on elongation depends on its catalytic activity.
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The effect of Ubp15 on elongation depends on its catalytic activity.
source: The ubp15-C214A mutant, but not the WT UBP15, rescued the dst1Δ and spt4Δ sensitivities to 6AU (Figure 2B), demonstrating that the effect of Ubp15 on elongation depends on its catalytic activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the complementation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ubp15Δ cells show sensitivity to cold temperature.
source: Noteworthy, we also looked at the phenotype of ubp15Δ cells under several other growth conditions and confirmed previously described sensitivity to cold temperature and hydroxyurea (HU) (Amerik et al., 2000; Ostapenko et al., 2015)
evidence: This is confirmed in the serial-dilution growth assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations to Amerik et al., 2000; Ostapenko et al., 2015.

claim: ubp15Δ cells show sensitivity to hydroxyurea (HU).
source: Noteworthy, we also looked at the phenotype of ubp15Δ cells under several other growth conditions and confirmed previously described sensitivity to cold temperature and hydroxyurea (HU) (Amerik et al., 2000; Ostapenko et al., 2015)
evidence: This is confirmed in the serial-dilution growth assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations to Amerik et al., 2000; Ostapenko et al., 2015.

claim: Elevated temperature, ultraviolet light, formamide or caffeine had no detectable effect on ubp15Δ cells.
source: while elevated temperature, ultraviolet light, formamide or caffeine had no detectable effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, elongation factors affect the processivity of RNAPII but have no measurable impact on the elongation rate.
source: In S. cerevisiae, elongation factors affect the processivity of RNAPII (i.e. the capacity of the polymerase to reach the end of the gene) but have no measurable impact on the elongation rate (Mason and Struhl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mason and Struhl, 2005.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 did not rescue the processivity defect of dst1Δ cells in the presence of 6AU.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the deletion of UBP15 did not rescue the processivity defect of dst1Δ cells in the presence of 6AU (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-qPCR analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: ChIP-chip experiments confirmed the processivity defect of dst1Δ cells.
source: These experiments confirmed the processivity defect of dst1Δ cells but, consistently with our ChIP-qPCR analysis of the YLR454W gene (Figure 3A), revealed no effect of UBP15 deletion on RNAPII processivity in WT or dst1Δ cells.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-chip experiments presented in Figure 3B.

claim: ChIP-chip experiments revealed no effect of UBP15 deletion on RNAPII processivity in WT or dst1Δ cells.
source: These experiments confirmed the processivity defect of dst1Δ cells but, consistently with our ChIP-qPCR analysis of the YLR454W gene (Figure 3A), revealed no effect of UBP15 deletion on RNAPII processivity in WT or dst1Δ cells.
evidence: This is shown in the ChIP-chip experiments presented in Figure 3B.

claim: UBP15 deletion may rescue the 6AU sensitivity of elongation factor mutants indirectly.
source: This result was somewhat unexpected given the genetic interactions described in Figure 2 and suggests that UBP15 deletion may rescue the 6AU sensitivity of elongation factor mutants indirectly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the processivity data.

claim: No elongation factor has been shown to affect elongation rate in yeast.
source: Alternatively, Ubp15 may affect elongation rate, a parameter not investigated here, but this appears unlikely since no elongation factor has been shown to affect this parameter in yeast (Mason and Struhl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mason and Struhl, 2005.

claim: A mutant of the E3 ligase Rsp5 (rsp5-1) exacerbated the 6AU sensitivity of dst1Δ cells.
source: Through testing several candidates (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), we noticed that a mutant of the E3 ligase Rsp5 (rsp5-1) exacerbated the 6AU sensitivity of dst1Δ cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The effect of rsp5-1 on the dst1Δ 6AU sensitivity is opposite to that of ubp15Δ.
source: This effect of rsp5-1 on the dst1Δ 6AU sensitivity is opposite to that of ubp15Δ (Figure 2A) suggesting that Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in regulating a process genetically connected to transcription elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in regulating a process genetically connected to transcription elongation.
source: This effect of rsp5-1 on the dst1Δ 6AU sensitivity is opposite to that of ubp15Δ (Figure 2A) suggesting that Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in regulating a process genetically connected to transcription elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 can partially rescue the 6AU sensitivity of rsp5-1/dst1Δ mutant.
source: Furthermore, the deletion of UBP15 can partially rescue the 6AU sensitivity of rsp5-1/dst1Δ mutant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 rescued the thermosensitivity phenotype of rsp5-ts mutants.
source: The antagonistic relationship between Rsp5 and Ubp15 is also supported by the fact that the deletion of UBP15 rescued the thermosensitivity phenotype of rsp5-ts mutants (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The rescue of rsp5-1 thermosensitivity by UBP15 deletion is dependent on the catalytic activity of Ubp15.
source: Importantly, the rescue of rsp5-1 thermosensitivity was also observed with the ubp15-C214A mutant indicating it is dependent on the catalytic activity of Ubp15 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of Rsp5-1 can rescue the rsp5-1 thermosensitivity phenotype.
source: Because we found that overexpression of Rps5-1 can rescue the rsp5-1 thermosensitivity phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), we next tested whether Rsp5 protein levels were affected by the deletion of UBP15.
evidence: This is shown in the serial-dilution growth assays presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rsp5 protein levels in rsp5-1 cells are decreased upon deletion of UBP15.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Rsp5 protein levels in rsp5-1 cells are actually decreased upon deletion of UBP15.
evidence: This is shown in the western blot presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: UBP15 deletion suppresses the rsp5-1 thermosensitivity phenotype by mechanisms other than increasing Rsp5 protein levels.
source: This result suggests that UBP15 deletion suppresses the rsp5-1 thermosensitivity phenotype by other mechanisms, as explored further below.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rsp5 levels decrease upon UBP15 deletion.

claim: Rsp5 is an E3 ligase involved in DNA damage.
source: Rsp5 is an E3 ligase involved in DNA damage (Beaudenon et al., 1999) and mRNA export (Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beaudenon et al., 1999.

claim: Rsp5 is an E3 ligase involved in mRNA export.

claim: At high temperatures, the rsp5-1 mutant accumulates mRNA in the nucleus.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2003.

claim: The suppression of mRNA export defect by UBP15 deletion likely explains how UBP15 deletion restored the viability of rsp5 mutants.

evidence: This is an inference based on the mRNA export data.

claim: Mex67 is a substrate of Ubp15.
source: These experiments identified Mex67 as a likely substrate of Ubp15 (Figure 5B,C).

claim: Mex67 ubiquitylation levels decreased in rsp5-1.
source: Interestingly, Mex67 ubiquitylation levels decreased in rsp5-1 (Figure 5B), suggesting that Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in the control of Mex67 ubiquitylation.

claim: Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in the control of Mex67 ubiquitylation.
source: Interestingly, Mex67 ubiquitylation levels decreased in rsp5-1 (Figure 5B), suggesting that Rsp5 and Ubp15 may oppose each other in the control of Mex67 ubiquitylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ubiquitylation data.

claim: The deletion of UBP15 normalized Mex67 ubiquitylation of rsp5-1 cells.
source: To assess this possibility more directly, we tested Mex67 ubiquitylation levels in ubp15Δ/rsp5-1 double mutant and found that the deletion of UBP15 normalized Mex67 ubiquitylation of rsp5-1 cells (Figure 5C).

claim: Rsp5 and Ubp15 function as an E3 ligase/deubiquitylase tandem regulating Mex67 ubiquitylation.
source: Collectively, these experiments established Rsp5 and Ubp15 as an E3 ligase/deubiquitylase tandem regulating Mex67 ubiquitylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ubiquitylation data.

claim: Mex67 is known to function as part of a large and dynamic protein interaction network.

evidence: This is established knowledge about Mex67.

claim: Mex67 ubiquitylation may modulate its interactome.
source: Since Mex67 is known to function as part of a large and dynamic protein interaction network, we hypothesized that its ubiquitylation may modulate its interactome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated explicitly.

claim: Mex67 interacts with Mtr2, Nab2, Yra2, the THO complex and nearly the entire NPC.
source: As expected, based on previous studies (Batisse et al., 2009; Gwizdek et al., 2006; Oeffinger et al., 2007; Santos-Rosa et al., 1998; Saroufim et al., 2015; Strässer and Hurt, 2000b; Zenklusen et al., 2001), we found a large number of Mex67-interacting proteins including Mtr2, Nab2, Yra2, the THO complex and nearly the entire NPC (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is confirmed by proteomic analysis and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Seven proteins were differentially associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells by at least twofold.
source: Among those, only seven were differentially associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells by at least twofold (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: All proteins differentially associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells were less associated with Mex67.
source: Interestingly, all those interactors were less associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells, suggesting that the ubiquitylation of Mex67 negatively regulates its association with these factors.
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The ubiquitylation of Mex67 negatively regulates its association with THO and CBC.
source: Interestingly, all those interactors were less associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells, suggesting that the ubiquitylation of Mex67 negatively regulates its association with these factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data showing decreased association in ubp15Δ cells where Mex67 is hyper-ubiquitylated.

claim: The proteins less associated with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells include all four subunits of the THO complex (Hpr1, Tho2, Mft1, and Thp2) and both subunits of the heterodimeric cap-binding complex (CBC; Sto1 and Cbc2).
source: Strikingly, these proteins include all four subunits of the THO complex (Hpr1, Tho2, Mft1, and Thp2) and both subunits of the heterodimeric cap-binding complex (CBC; Sto1 and Cbc2) known to recruit THO/TREX to the 5'-cap of nascent pre-mRNAs (Figure 5D) in yeast and humans (Cheng et al., 2006; Sen et al., 2019; Viphakone et al., 2019).

claim: CBC is known to recruit THO/TREX to the 5'-cap of nascent pre-mRNAs in yeast and humans.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2006; Sen et al., 2019; Viphakone et al., 2019.

claim: Several subunits of the NPC, including the nuclear basket protein Mlp1, showed a slightly increased association with Mex67 in ubp15Δ cells compared to WT cells.

evidence: This is shown in the proteomic analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Mex67 ubiquitylation, controlled by Rsp5 and Ubp15, regulates the association of Mex67 to pre-mRNAs via interactions with THO and cap binding factors.

evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data.

source: In principle, one possible role of Mex67 ubiquitylation/deubiquitylation by Rsp5 and Ubp15, respectively, could be to regulate its nuclear localization. However, we could not observe any effect of ubp15Δ or rsp5-1 mutants on Mex67 localization by immunofluorescence (Mex67 localized at the nuclear envelope in all strains tested, data not shown).

claim: Mex67 localization is restricted to the NPC.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Derrer et al., 2019.
